name: Visions of Mars
operator: The Planetary Society, with IKI and NASA
short_status: On Mars since 25 May 2008 and still unread: a Planetary Society disc of about 80 Mars works, bolted to the Phoenix lander deck at 68.22 N, 234.25 E. The first copy was lost with Mars 96 in November 1996.
tagline: The Planetary Society, with IKI and NASA · Multinational · Artefact · 2008 · The long occupation Success
stats: stories, essays and articles about Mars encoded on the disc
flights: destroyed with Mars 96 in 1996, landed with Phoenix in 2008
names of members and members of the public riding on the Phoenix copy

facts.label: Whose idea it was
facts.value: Louis Friedman, executive director of The Planetary Society, raised the concept in 1991 with the Society's president Carl Sagan and vice president Bruce Murray. They took it to the Institute for Space Research (IKI) in Moscow, which was building the lander for what was then the Mars 94 mission and later became Mars 96. Friedman's first proposal was modest: one work each by Isaac Asimov, Ray Bradbury and Arthur C. Clarke, which he called the science fiction ABC, and the project's first internal name was Project ABC.

facts.label: The original object
facts.value: An 8 cm CD-ROM, produced by Time Warner Interactive Group, with Jim Bumgardner as producer, Stephen Johnson as art and design director, Blake Lewin as project manager, Cynthia Woll as editorial director and Esther Gwynne as editor. Bumgardner wrote a page-turning book interface for it; the text was proofed and copy-edited in eight languages. The disc's title screen carries the name of Mars in a range of Earth languages, echoing the convention by which the Martian valles are named for the planet in different cultures.

facts.label: Who chose the contents
facts.value: Editorially the project ran out of the Merril Collection of Science Fiction, Speculation and Fantasy in Toronto, the public library founded on Judith Merril's donated collection and originally called the Spaced Out Library. Merril wrote or expanded most of the story introductions. Jon Lomberg, who had been design director for the Voyager Golden Record, directed and edited the project; John Robert Colombo built the candidate lists; Lorna Toolis, head of the Merril Collection, ran the acquisition and fact checking. Selections were sent to Carl Sagan for review.

facts.label: What is on it
facts.value: The Planetary Society's own description runs to Percival Lowell expounding the canals, H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds, Isaac Asimov, Ray Bradbury, Poul Anderson and many others, each story carrying an introduction, with a glossary and a short history of the twentieth century written for a reader who will not share our references. There is a collection of rare Mars artwork, the recording of Orson Welles's 1938 radio broadcast of The War of the Worlds, and Bob Derkach's composition The Winds of Mars, written after consulting the atmospheric scientist James Pollack on how wind might sound in air that thin.

facts.label: How international it is, and the disagreement about it
facts.value: The Planetary Society's own numbers do not agree. Its page listing the texts says the authors represent 22 nationalities and cultures and names them, including Babylonian and Inuit. Its press release of 22 May 2008 says 20 nations and cultures. Its press release of 27 May 2008 says nearly 30. The 22 figure is the one attached to an actual list, so it is the one to prefer.

facts.label: The voices
facts.value: The disc carries recorded messages to future Martians from Carl Sagan, filmed near his home in Ithaca, New York, from Arthur C. Clarke at home in Sri Lanka, from Louis Friedman at the Society's headquarters in Pasadena, and, added for the 2008 version, from Phoenix principal investigator Peter Smith. The team had wanted video greetings; the 1990s disc could not hold moving pictures, so Lomberg and Stephen Johnson converted them into stills and audio.

facts.label: Engineering it to survive
facts.value: The Society hired Gene Giberson, a recently retired JPL assistant laboratory director who had managed the Surveyor lunar programme, Mariner 10, Seasat and IRAS, to qualify the disc for flight. He tested candidate materials against launch loads, a hard landing, Martian cold, chemical attack on the metallic layer by the atmosphere, radiation from the lander's power units and cosmic rays, and against planetary protection sterilisation requirements. Denis Oudard of the French disc manufacturer Digipress and Michael Stamp at Sony's plant in Terre Haute, Indiana advised and supplied test discs.

facts.label: The names rode on the outside
facts.value: The Planetary Society mounted MAPEX, a microelectronics and photonics experiment carrying the names of 100,000 of its members, onto the surface of the Mars 96 compact disc before the package was shipped to Russia. When Mars 96 was lost, a spare MAPEX chip went to Mars on Pathfinder in 1997 while Visions of Mars waited another eleven years for a ride.

facts.label: How it was lost the first time
facts.value: Mars 96 launched on 16 November 1996 at 20:48:53 UTC and was stranded in low Earth orbit when the Blok D-2 upper stage failed to make its second burn. It re-entered between about 00:30 and 01:30 UTC on 17 November along a track running from the eastern Pacific across northern Chile and Bolivia. A 2026 review by Dante Sanaei in The Space Review states that no search was ever conducted and the wreckage has never been found.

facts.label: How many copies were aboard Mars 96
facts.value: Unresolved. The Mars 96 spacecraft carried two small autonomous surface stations, either of which could in principle have taken a disc, and secondary accounts from 1996 refer to a copy on each of the two small landers. The Planetary Society's own writing about the loss, including Jon Lomberg's project history and its catalogue of flown messages, always speaks of the disk in the singular and never gives a number, so we do not state one.

facts.label: The second object
facts.value: For the 2007 flight the contents were reformatted and remixed onto an archival silica glass mini-DVD, an effort led by Bruce Betts at The Planetary Society. The Society provided the disc at no cost to NASA; engineering support came from Visionary Products, Inc., and Plasmon OMS donated the discs and the data writing. Lomberg's afterword notes that the format and contents of the original CD were deliberately retained, so what landed on Mars is a 1996 artefact reissued on 2007 media.

facts.label: The label
facts.value: The disc's label is addressed to whoever finds it. The Planetary Society's release of 27 May 2008, reporting the first images of the disc on the ground, states that the label reads "Attention Astronauts: Take This with You" and that it is legible in the images.

facts.label: How long it is expected to last
facts.value: The Society's figures vary with the audience. Its release of 22 May 2008 says the disc was expected to endure about 500 years on Mars. Its Phoenix DVD project page says the silica glass disc was designed to last hundreds if not thousands of years. Peter Smith's introduction on the disc itself makes the sharper point that the technology will be obsolete within twenty years even if the object survives for millennia.

facts.label: Where it is now
facts.value: On the deck of the Phoenix lander at 68.22 N, 234.25 E, about a metre above the arctic plain. Phoenix entered safe mode on 28 October 2008 as a dust storm cut its power, sent its last signal on 2 November 2008, and NASA formally ended the mission on 24 May 2010 after four listening campaigns and HiRISE images suggesting the solar panels had collapsed under carbon dioxide ice. Nothing has come from the site since, and nothing we consulted on 24 August 2026 suggests otherwise.

facts.label: The library claim
facts.value: The Planetary Society called it the first library on Mars and headed its 27 May 2008 release Phoenix Takes Image of First Library on Mars. That is the Society's claim about its own object and we report it as such. We have not attempted to verify any broader superlative about libraries on other worlds, and note that other collections have been sent to the Moon by other organisations.

timeline: Louis Friedman raises the idea with Carl Sagan and Bruce Murray, and The Planetary Society approaches IKI in Moscow about putting a disc on the Mars 94 lander. The working title is Project ABC, for Asimov, Bradbury and Clarke.

The disc is cut at Time Warner Interactive with the Merril Collection in Toronto as its editorial base, and the team presents the project at that year's International Astronautical Congress as a cultural and scientific experiment on Mars 96. The congress presentation is not described on the Lomberg project history cited here and needs its own source before publication.
Mars 96 launches at 20:48:53 UTC and is stranded in low Earth orbit when the Blok D-2 upper stage does not make its second burn.

The spacecraft re-enters between about 00:30 and 01:30 UTC along a track from the eastern Pacific across northern Chile and Bolivia, taking the first copy of Visions of Mars with it. No search is ever mounted.
Carl Sagan dies, five weeks after the loss. His recorded message to future Martians, made for the disc, survives and flies on the second copy.
The spare MAPEX chip, which had been mounted on the surface of the lost disc and carried 100,000 Planetary Society member names, reaches Mars aboard Pathfinder. Visions of Mars does not.

Bruce Betts leads the reformatting of the 1996 contents onto an archival silica glass mini-DVD, with 250,000 names added and the original format and selection deliberately preserved. Plasmon OMS donates the discs and the writing.
Phoenix launches from Cape Canaveral at 09:26:34 UT with the disc bolted to its deck.
Phoenix lands at 68.22 N, 234.25 E in the arctic plains. Visions of Mars arrives on Mars eleven and a half years after its first attempt.

The Surface Stereo Imager returns the first pictures of the disc lying on the deck, its label legible. Louis Friedman says seeing it there culminates fifteen years of effort; Bruce Betts says the team is ecstatic.

Phoenix sends its last signal on 2 November as the arctic autumn takes its sunlight, and NASA declares the surface mission finished on 10 November. The disc has been sitting on a dead lander ever since.

After more than 200 Mars Odyssey overflights across four listening campaigns produce nothing, NASA formally ends the mission. HiRISE imagery indicates the solar panels have collapsed under carbon dioxide ice.

images.caption: The silica glass mini-DVD photographed against a plain background on Earth, its label reading Messages from Earth, Phoenix, 2007, Attention Astronauts: Take This with You, and at the foot Visions of Mars: First Library on Mars, with a painting of a row of old books at the left, a swirled Mars motif at the right, a paragraph of explanatory text below the hub, and the names of the University of Arizona, Lockheed Martin, NASA and JPL running around the rim.

The title screen of the Visions of Mars disc as The Planetary Society publishes it on its 2007 Phoenix credits page: a rendered Mars against black with the words Visions of Mars across it, ringed by the name of the planet written in a dozen other scripts, among them Sanskrit, Cyrillic, Korean, Chinese, Hebrew, Thai, Greek and Arabic.

A Surface Stereo Imager view down onto the Phoenix lander deck in the first days after landing, with the mini-DVD lying flat at the lower left, its label and the words Attention Astronauts: Take This with You legible, a small United States flag beside it, a solar panel at the upper left and the rock strewn arctic plain filling the rest of the frame.

A vertical projection assembled from hundreds of Surface Stereo Imager exposures, showing the whole Phoenix lander from overhead with both circular solar arrays spread, the instrument deck between them and the black disc where the camera's own mounting blocks the view. The mini-DVD is bolted to this deck, next to the small flag near the lower edge of the lander body.
